newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says Haiti elections were free and fair.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says Haiti elections were free and fair.

text.p: The United States, which has invested much in Haiti's experiment with democracy, on Monday said weekend elections were free and fair and an important step forward despite the low voter turnout.
Washington also praised Haiti's national police for implementing a "thorough" election security plan.
Nine seats in the 27-seat Senate, two parliamentary seats and nearly 700 local positions were up for grabs in Sunday's polls.

Although more than four million Haitians were registered, only handfuls turned up at many polling stations to vote. Observers reported a de facto boycott by voters, frustrated by continued hardship and poverty despite the ouster of the former military regime.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns brushed off the low voter turnout, saying "that sometimes happens in the United States as well for local elections ... and town elections, municipal elections."
"...we believe these elections were an important step in the process of consolidating democracy in Haiti," he said.

"These were the fifth elections since democracy was restored in 1994. And they, we hope, will contribute to a decentralization of political power in Haiti by bringing democratic rule to the local level for the very first time."
Burns acknowledged "scattered reports of outside interference in the electoral process" but he said election authorities and the Haitian national police were able to resolve each case.

"Available reports to us, including from our embassy, indicate the elections were free and fair, and were open," he said, adding: "So we think the elections were a positive development ... And the important thing is that the dictators never allowed people to vote; now they can. And people are responsible for their own democracy."
Despite the administration's positive assessment of the poll, a U.S. observer team said it was a "lost opportunity" that set back efforts to make democracy take root in Haiti.

The low turnout indicated frustration and disillusionment among the electorate, Utah Lt. Gov. Olene Walker, leader of the International Republican Institute delegation, told a news briefing on Monday.

"Such sentiments, which appear to be widespread, are not encouraging for Haiti's democratic development," Walker said. "The weak turnout severely undermines the process begun in 1990 and now places an even greater responsibility on Haiti's government and all the nation's leaders to overcome yesterday's lost opportunity."

Some U.S. news reports criticised the way Haitian national police handled election security but Burns disputed that, saying the police "implemented a thorough election security plan, which helped assure that the elections would take place in a peaceful and orderly manner."

The United States sent 20,000 troops to Haiti in September 1994 as part of a plan that restored then-President Jean Bertrand Aristide to power and ousted the military regime that had overthrown Aristide in a bloody 1991 coup.
